text: The Sámi are the Indigenous people of Sápmi, the far north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.
For more than 2,000 years they have fished, hunted, trapped and traded furs there.
src: The Sámi are the Indigenous people of Sápmi / northern Norway, Sweden and Finland and the Kola Peninsula of Russia / their land Sápmi

Arrived in Sápmi in the Bronze Age or early Iron Age (2nd–1st millennia BCE) / For most of their history they lived by fishing, hunting, trapping and trade / The Sámi traded hides and furs for salt, metal blades and coins

text: About 500 years ago, many settled by the coast and kept cattle, sheep and goats.
Some began herding reindeer, and today about one Sámi in ten is connected to herding.
src: Around 1500 / Most Sámi then settled along fjords, coasts and inland rivers, combining fishing and trapping with cattle, sheep and goats
while a minority tamed reindeer and became the reindeer nomads / today about one Sámi in ten is connected to it

text: Nearby kingdoms taxed them, and Sweden forced some Sámi to work at a silver mine.
Missionaries burned their sacred drums, and later the Sámi language was banned in Norway’s schools.
src: Denmark–Norway, Sweden and Russia all claimed the right to tax the Sámi / the Swedish crown forced Swedish conscripts and Sámi cart drivers to work at the Nasa silver mine

the missionary Thomas von Westen led a campaign around 1720 that burned drums and destroyed sacred sites / From the 1860s Norway turned to Norwegianisation: from around 1900 Sámi could not be used in public school or in church

text: Today the Sámi have their own parliaments, a flag and a national day.
Their gákti clothes, often of wool or cotton, show by their colours where the wearer comes from.
src: Sámi Parliaments were founded in Finland (1973), Norway (1989) and Sweden (1993) / The Sámi flag, designed by Astrid Båhl, was adopted in 1986, and 6 February became Sámi National Day
Gákti, once made of reindeer leather and sinew and now more often of wool, cotton or silk / the colours, patterns and jewellery of the gákti show where the wearer comes from
